query: How are coronary artery calcifications associated with complications?
draft_answer: Across the included studies, coronary artery calcification appears to be associated with worse clinical outcomes, but the strength and type of outcome vary by setting [pmc_PMC5383538||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9806039||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10229702||ABSTRACT||001]. In a review, CAC was associated with future ASCVD risk independent of conventional risk factors and improved risk prediction when added to a global model such as the Framingham risk score [pmc_PMC5383538||ABSTRACT||000]. In symptomatic patients referred for cardiac CT, higher CAC scores were associated with all-cause mortality risk, although MESA percentile measures did not outperform absolute CAC for prediction [pmc_PMC9806039||ABSTRACT||000]. In level-1 trauma patients, coronary artery calcification visible on routine CT was independently associated with in-hospital complications, and left main coronary calcification in particular was associated with any complication [pmc_PMC10229702||ABSTRACT||001]. The number of calcified coronary arteries also trended toward association with complications and was significantly associated with adverse discharge condition, while pulmonary emphysema and aortic calcifications were not associated with complications in that study [pmc_PMC10229702||ABSTRACT||001]. By contrast, two papers provided no direct evidence linking coronary artery calcification to complications in their study populations, and one specifically stated that the evidence was insufficient to connect CAC with recurrent hospitalization or post-revascularization prognosis [pmc_PMC10140970||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9806495||ABSTRACT||000]. Another study of heavily calcified coronary lesions reported favorable short-term procedural outcomes with no primary safety events at 30 days, suggesting that severe calcification does not necessarily imply immediate procedural complications in that context [pmc_PMC10140256||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence supports an association between CAC and adverse outcomes, but the complications studied differ substantially across papers and the findings are not uniform across clinical contexts [pmc_PMC5383538||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9806039||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10229702||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: CAC is associated with future ASCVD risk independent of conventional risk factors and improves risk prediction when added to a global model [pmc_PMC5383538||ABSTRACT||000].

Higher CAC scores were associated with all-cause mortality risk in symptomatic patients referred for cardiac CT, although percentile-based measures did not improve prediction over absolute CAC [pmc_PMC9806039||ABSTRACT||000].

In level-1 trauma patients, coronary artery calcification on routine CT was independently associated with in-hospital complications, especially left main coronary calcification [pmc_PMC10229702||ABSTRACT||001].

The number of calcified coronary arteries was associated with adverse discharge condition in the trauma study and showed a trend toward association with complications [pmc_PMC10229702||ABSTRACT||001].
A study of heavily calcified coronary lesions reported no primary safety events during 30 days of follow-up despite substantial calcification burden [pmc_PMC10140256||ABSTRACT||001].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The papers examine different outcomes—ASCVD risk, mortality, trauma complications, recurrent hospitalization, and procedural safety—so the evidence is not directly comparable across settings [pmc_PMC5383538||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9806039||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10229702||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC10140970||ABSTRACT||000].

Some summaries explicitly state that evidence is insufficient or does not mention CAC, limiting how broadly the association with complications can be generalized [pmc_PMC10140970||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9806495||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC8758654||ABSTRACT||000].

At least one study suggests severe calcification may not lead to short-term procedural safety events, indicating that CAC does not uniformly predict immediate complications in all clinical contexts [pmc_PMC10140256||ABSTRACT||001].
